strings.name: Shigeru Ban
strings.summary: Born in Japan, Ban trained in architecture in the United States before founding a practice in Tokyo. He explores structures made from paper tubes, timber and recyclable materials, extending design into temporary housing and public facilities after disasters. His work includes museums, houses and churches, often developed with international teams. The Pritzker Prize and AIA Gold Medal recognize his structural innovation and sustained humanitarian work.
strings.coverageNote: Selected verifiable milestones through June 2026; checked on 13 November 2026. Collaborative buildings retain team attribution; future exhibition plans are not presented as completed events.
strings.influence.rationale: He applies materials such as paper tubes to architecture and temporary post-disaster housing, connecting design innovation, humanitarian relief and architects’ public responsibility.

strings.facts.f2.label: Education
strings.facts.f2.value: Studies at SCI-Arc; Bachelor of Architecture, Cooper Union (1984)
strings.highlights.h1.title: Materials and structures
strings.highlights.h1.text: Uses paper tubes and timber in houses, cultural buildings and relief facilities, emphasizing accessible materials.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Architecture after disasters
strings.highlights.h2.text: Founded the Voluntary Architects’ Network in 1995, involving local residents, students and volunteers in post-disaster construction.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Recognized with the AIA Gold Medal
strings.timeline.t1.text: Honored at the AIA conference in San Diego, where he spoke about connections between design and social responsibility.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Receives the Pritzker Prize
strings.timeline.t2.text: The Pritzker Architecture Prize recognized experimental materials, structural innovation and sustained service to disaster-affected communities.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Cardboard Cathedral opens
strings.timeline.t3.text: Christchurch’s Transitional Cathedral opened, using paper tubes and other materials to address religious and community needs after the earthquake.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Centre Pompidou-Metz opens
strings.timeline.t4.text: Completed the museum with Jean de Gastines; Philip Gumuchdjian contributed to the winning competition design.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Japan Pavilion at Hanover Expo
strings.timeline.t5.text: Collaborated with Frei Otto on a paper-tube grid shell, exploring material recycling and structural possibilities for a large pavilion.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Founds the Voluntary Architects’ Network
strings.timeline.t6.text: Built paper-tube temporary houses and a paper church after the Kobe earthquake and organized VAN for relief work.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Starts a practice in Tokyo
strings.timeline.t7.text: Established an independent practice, developing structural research into everyday materials through exhibition design and experimental houses.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Completes an architecture degree
strings.timeline.t8.text: Graduated from Cooper Union after studying at SCI-Arc and working in Arata Isozaki’s office.
strings.timeline.t9.title: Born in Tokyo
strings.timeline.t9.text: Watching carpenters repair his family home sparked an early interest in woodwork and models, followed by a decision to study architecture.
